subject: economics
description: Economics question bank, FET (CAPS Grades 10-12). Keyed by atomic skill id. Each pool targets 20 items, FET pass mark 0.6, no timer. Cognitive mix per CAPS: ~30% Knowledge/Comprehension (difficulty 1), ~40% Application/Analysis (difficulty 2), ~30% Synthesis/Evaluation (difficulty 3). Tap-based mechanics only (no free-text): choice, true-false, cloze, sequence, diagram-label (graph reading), sort-buckets, paragraph-template and source-comparison. Authored from data/economics-authoring/grade{10,11,12}.mjs via scripts/gen-economics-bank.mjs.

ECON.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.title: Economics: basic concepts & methods
ECON.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.description: What economics is, its branches (micro/macro) and approaches; positive vs normative statements, the scientific method, the use of models, and economics' links to other disciplines and careers.
ECON.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Macroeconomics: basic concepts, the economic problem & the circular flow
ECON.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: A positive statement can be tested as true or false; a normative statement is a value judgement ('should/ought').

questions.question: Economics is best described as the study of how people use…
options: scarce resources to satisfy needs and wants
questions.expected: scarce resources to satisfy needs and wants
questions.memo: Economics studies how scarce resources are used to satisfy unlimited needs and wants.

questions.question: The branch of economics that looks at the whole economy (e.g. total output, inflation) is…
questions.memo: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole; microeconomics studies single markets.

questions.question: The branch that studies a single market, like the market for bread, is…
questions.memo: Micro = small parts (one market, one firm); macro = the big picture.

questions.question: A statement that can be tested as true or false is a ______ statement.
questions.memo: Positive statements are factual and testable; normative statements are opinions.

questions.question: A statement that gives an opinion about what 'should' happen is a ______ statement.
questions.memo: Normative statements contain a value judgement ('should', 'ought').

questions.question: 'The unemployment rate is 33%' is a positive statement.
questions.memo: It states a fact that can be checked, so it is positive.

questions.question: Which of these is a normative statement?
options: The government should spend more on schools
questions.expected: The government should spend more on schools
questions.memo: 'Should' signals an opinion — a normative statement.

questions.question: Economists use simplified 'models' mainly to…
options: explain and predict how the economy works
questions.expected: explain and predict how the economy works
questions.memo: A model simplifies reality so we can understand and predict it.

questions.question: Studying the economy is harder than a lab science mainly because…
options: you cannot run controlled experiments on a whole economy
questions.expected: you cannot run controlled experiments on a whole economy
questions.memo: Social sciences struggle to control all the variables a lab can.

questions.question: Which subject is most closely linked to Economics in working out interest and growth?
questions.memo: Maths is used for calculations like interest, growth rates and indices.

questions.question: Sort each statement as positive or normative.

items.text: The rich ought to pay more tax

questions.memo: Facts you can check are positive; opinions about what 'should' be are normative.

questions.question: Sort each topic as macroeconomics or microeconomics.

items.text: The price of one shop's bread
How one firm sets its output

questions.memo: Whole-economy topics are macro; single-market topics are micro.

questions.question: A career that uses Economics directly would be…
questions.memo: Economics opens careers like analyst, economist, banker and policy advisor.

questions.question: Economics only studies money.
questions.memo: Economics studies all scarce resources and choices, not just money.

questions.question: An economist says: 'If tax rises, people will spend less.' This is mainly…
options: a positive prediction that can be tested
questions.expected: a positive prediction that can be tested
questions.memo: It predicts a measurable outcome, so it is positive.

questions.question: Why might two economists disagree even when they use the same facts?
options: They hold different normative values about what should be done
questions.expected: They hold different normative values about what should be done
questions.memo: Shared facts can still lead to different value-based recommendations.

questions.question: A model of the economy is useful even though it is simplified because…
options: it focuses on the key relationships and ignores the noise
it copies every detail of reality
it removes the need for data
questions.expected: it focuses on the key relationships and ignores the noise
questions.memo: Good models strip away detail to reveal the main forces at work.

questions.question: Which pairing of branch and question is correct?
options: Macro — what price should one bakery charge?
Micro — how fast is the whole economy growing?
Micro — what is the national unemployment rate?
questions.memo: National inflation is an economy-wide (macro) question.

questions.question: Treating the business as separate from the country's whole economy is the difference between…
questions.memo: One firm = micro; the whole economy = macro.

questions.question: Build a short answer on why economists use models.
questions.prompt: Why do economists use models?

options.text: A model is a simplified picture of the economy
A model is a perfect copy of the economy
It shows the main links, like how price affects quantity
It lists every single transaction in the country
So we can explain and predict outcomes without being overwhelmed by detail
So the economy becomes more complicated to study

questions.memo: A model simplifies reality to help explain and predict.

ECON.G10.T1.SCARCITY.A1.title: Scarcity & the economic problem
ECON.G10.T1.SCARCITY.A1.description: Absolute vs relative scarcity, economic vs free goods, choice and opportunity cost, and the basic processes of production, exchange and consumption.
ECON.G10.T1.SCARCITY.A1.strand: Term 1 — Macroeconomics: basic concepts, the economic problem & the circular flow
ECON.G10.T1.SCARCITY.A1.recovery_strategy: Opportunity cost = the value of the NEXT-BEST option you gave up, not the rand price.

questions.question: Scarcity exists because…
options: needs and wants are unlimited but resources are limited
questions.expected: needs and wants are unlimited but resources are limited
questions.memo: Scarcity is the gap between unlimited wants and limited resources.

questions.question: The next-best alternative you give up when you make a choice is the ______.
questions.memo: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option foregone.

questions.question: An economic good is one that…
options: is scarce and has a price
questions.expected: is scarce and has a price
questions.memo: Economic goods are scarce, so they have a price; free goods are unlimited.

questions.question: Which of these is closest to a free good?
questions.memo: A free good is so abundant it has no price — like ordinary air.

questions.question: Because resources are scarce, every choice has an opportunity cost.
questions.memo: Choosing one thing means giving up the next-best thing.

questions.question: Making, growing or providing goods and services is called ______.
questions.memo: Production creates goods and services; consumption uses them up.

questions.question: A learner can either study OR watch TV for the next hour. If she studies, her opportunity cost is…
options: the hour of TV she gives up
the cost of the TV set
questions.expected: the hour of TV she gives up
questions.memo: Opportunity cost is the next-best activity foregone — watching TV.

questions.question: Using up goods and services to satisfy wants is called…
questions.memo: Consumption is the final use of goods and services.

questions.question: Trading or buying and selling goods and services is called…
questions.memo: Exchange moves goods between people, usually using money.

questions.question: Sort each item as an economic good or a free good.
questions.memo: Economic goods are scarce and priced; free goods are unlimited and unpriced.

questions.question: Sort each activity into production, exchange or consumption.

items.text: Buying the bread at a shop

questions.memo: Make it (production), trade it (exchange), use it (consumption).

questions.question: Government has R1 million and can build a clinic OR a library, not both. The opportunity cost of the clinic is…
questions.memo: Opportunity cost is the next-best option given up — the library.

questions.question: If something has a price, it is an economic (scarce) good.
questions.memo: Prices arise because the good is scarce.

questions.question: Absolute scarcity means…
options: there is simply not enough of the resource for everyone
questions.expected: there is simply not enough of the resource for everyone
questions.memo: Absolute scarcity = a fixed, limited total no matter the price.

questions.question: Why does scarcity force people and governments to make choices?
options: Because they cannot have everything they want at once
questions.expected: Because they cannot have everything they want at once
questions.memo: Limited resources versus unlimited wants forces choice.

questions.question: A country spends more on weapons and less on hospitals. The clearest opportunity cost is…
options: the hospital care that is now not provided
questions.expected: the hospital care that is now not provided
questions.memo: The next-best use of those funds — health care — is foregone.

questions.question: Which statement about free goods is correct?
options: They are unlimited, so no choice or price is needed for them
They are the cheapest goods in the shop
They are made only by government
questions.expected: They are unlimited, so no choice or price is needed for them
questions.memo: Truly free goods are abundant enough that no one must choose or pay.

questions.question: Opportunity cost is always measured in rands.
questions.memo: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative given up — often time or another good, not a rand amount.

questions.question: Put the basic economic processes in their natural order.
questions.memo: Goods are made, then traded, then used up.

questions.question: Build a short answer on opportunity cost.
questions.prompt: What is opportunity cost?

options.text: Opportunity cost is the next-best option you give up
Opportunity cost is the money in your pocket
If you spend an hour studying, you give up an hour of rest
If you study, you keep both the study time and the rest
Because resources are scarce, every choice means giving something up
Because resources are unlimited, nothing is given up

questions.memo: Opportunity cost = the next-best alternative foregone.

ECON.G10.T1.CIRCFLOW.A1.title: The circular flow model
ECON.G10.T1.CIRCFLOW.A1.description: Participants (households, firms, government, foreign sector), product and factor markets, the real and money flows between them, and leakages and injections in an open economy.
ECON.G10.T1.CIRCFLOW.A1.strand: Term 1 — Macroeconomics: basic concepts, the economic problem & the circular flow
ECON.G10.T1.CIRCFLOW.A1.recovery_strategy: Leakages (S, T, M) flow OUT of the circular flow; injections (I, G, X) flow IN.

questions.question: In the circular flow, households supply factors of production and receive…
questions.memo: Households sell factors and earn factor income in return.

questions.question: In the circular flow, firms produce goods and services and sell them in the…
questions.memo: Goods and services are bought and sold in the product market.

questions.question: Money that leaves the circular flow (savings, taxes, imports) is called a ______.
questions.memo: Leakages (S, T, M) withdraw money from the flow.

questions.question: Money that enters the circular flow (investment, government spending, exports) is an ______.
questions.memo: Injections (I, G, X) add money to the flow.

questions.question: Households and firms are two of the participants in the circular flow.
questions.memo: The four participants are households, firms, government and the foreign sector.

questions.question: Factors of production (land, labour, capital) are bought and sold in the…
questions.memo: The factor market is where the factors of production are traded.

questions.question: On the circular flow diagram, which arrow shows the MONEY flow from households to firms?

source.caption: Four-sector circular flow with real and money flows.

questions.memo: Households pay money to firms when they buy goods — a money flow.

questions.question: On the diagram, which is a REAL flow (not money)?

source.caption: Four-sector circular flow with real and money flows.

questions.memo: Real flows are goods and factors; money flows are payments.

questions.question: Which participant adds the foreign sector to the circular flow?
options: Exports and imports with other countries
questions.expected: Exports and imports with other countries
questions.memo: The foreign sector trades exports and imports with the economy.

questions.question: Sort each item as a leakage or an injection.
questions.memo: Leakages: saving, taxes, imports. Injections: investment, government spending, exports.

questions.question: Sort each into the product market or the factor market.
questions.memo: Goods/services = product market; factors of production = factor market.

questions.question: If households save more, the leakage from the flow…
questions.memo: Saving is a leakage, so more saving means a bigger leakage.

questions.question: Exports are an injection into the circular flow.
questions.memo: Exports bring foreign money into the economy — an injection.

questions.question: The government enters the circular flow mainly by…
questions.memo: Government takes taxes (leakage) and spends (injection).

questions.question: Why must the circular flow 'balance' over time?
options: Total income earned equals total spending in the economy
questions.expected: Total income earned equals total spending in the economy
questions.memo: Every rand of spending becomes someone's income, so the flows match.

questions.question: If injections are greater than leakages, the economy will tend to…
questions.memo: More money entering than leaving expands the flow — growth.

questions.question: Which correctly matches a flow with its direction?
options: Firms pay wages to households (money flow)
questions.expected: Firms pay wages to households (money flow)
questions.memo: Firms pay households for the factors they supply.

questions.question: A closed economy has no foreign sector in its circular flow.
questions.memo: A closed economy does not trade with the rest of the world.

questions.question: Trace the money: a household buys bread, then the firm uses the income to pay a worker. Put it in order.
options: Household spends in product market → firm earns revenue → firm pays wages in factor market
Firm pays wages → household spends → firm earns revenue
Firm earns revenue → household spends → firm pays wages
Household earns wages → firm spends → household pays revenue
questions.expected: Household spends in product market → firm earns revenue → firm pays wages in factor market
questions.memo: Spending becomes the firm's revenue, which becomes household income again.

questions.question: Build a short answer on leakages and injections.
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a leakage and an injection?

options.text: Leakages take money out of the flow; injections add money in
Leakages and injections are exactly the same thing
Saving, tax and imports leak out; investment, government spending and exports inject in
Exports leak out and imports inject in
When injections exceed leakages the economy grows, and the reverse shrinks it
Leakages and injections never affect the size of the economy

questions.memo: Leakages (S, T, M) withdraw; injections (I, G, X) add.

ECON.G10.T1.GDP.A1.title: GDP & GNI (quantitative)
ECON.G10.T1.GDP.A1.description: Defining and deriving GDP and GNI, their composition, importance and comparison; reading simple national-accounts figures.
ECON.G10.T1.GDP.A1.strand: Term 1 — Macroeconomics: basic concepts, the economic problem & the circular flow
ECON.G10.T1.GDP.A1.recovery_strategy: GDP = produced INSIDE the borders; GNI = earned BY the country's citizens, wherever they are.

questions.question: GDP stands for Gross ______ Product.
questions.memo: GDP = Gross Domestic Product — output produced inside the country.

questions.question: GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced…
options: inside a country's borders in a year
questions.expected: inside a country's borders in a year
questions.memo: GDP counts production within the borders, whoever owns the firm.

questions.question: GNI (Gross National Income) measures income earned by…
options: a country's citizens, wherever they are
questions.expected: a country's citizens, wherever they are
questions.memo: GNI follows the nationality of the earner, not the location.

questions.question: A higher GDP usually means more goods and services were produced.
questions.memo: GDP rising generally means more output.

questions.question: A foreign-owned factory produces cars in South Africa. That output is counted in SA's…
questions.memo: Production inside the borders counts in GDP regardless of owner.

questions.question: A South African working in London earns a salary. That income is part of SA's…
questions.memo: A citizen's income abroad counts in GNI, not GDP.

questions.question: GDP measured before subtracting wear-and-tear on capital is called ______ domestic product.
questions.memo: 'Gross' means before deducting depreciation; 'net' is after.

questions.question: If a country's GDP is R5 000bn and citizens earn R200bn abroad while foreigners earn R150bn locally, GNI is roughly…
questions.memo: GNI = GDP + income from abroad − income paid abroad = 5 000 + 200 − 150.

questions.question: GDP and GNI are always exactly equal.
questions.memo: They differ by the net income flowing to/from the rest of the world.

questions.question: Sort each item: counted in GDP (produced inside SA) or not?

items.text: Maize grown on a SA farm
A SA citizen's wages earned in Dubai
Cars built at a SA plant

questions.memo: GDP counts production located inside the borders only.

questions.question: Why is GDP useful?
options: It is a broad measure of the size of an economy
questions.expected: It is a broad measure of the size of an economy
questions.memo: GDP gauges total economic activity and the economy's size.

questions.question: GDP per person (per capita) is found by…
questions.memo: GDP per capita = GDP ÷ population — output per person.

questions.question: A country's GDP is R6 000bn and its population is 60 million. GDP per capita is…
questions.memo: R6 000bn ÷ 60 million = R100 000 per person.

questions.question: Two countries with the same GDP can have very different GDP per person.
questions.memo: A larger population spreads the same GDP more thinly per person.

questions.question: Which is the best simple definition of GDP?
options: The total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a year
The total money in the banks
questions.expected: The total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a year
questions.memo: GDP = value of all final output produced domestically in a period.

questions.question: A big limitation of GDP as a measure of wellbeing is that it…
options: ignores how income is shared and unpaid work
questions.expected: ignores how income is shared and unpaid work
questions.memo: GDP says nothing about inequality, the environment or unpaid work.

questions.question: If GDP rises but the population rises faster, GDP per person…
questions.memo: When population grows faster than GDP, output per person drops.

questions.question: GDP that is adjusted to remove the effect of price rises is called ______ GDP.
questions.memo: Real GDP strips out inflation; nominal GDP does not.

questions.question: Which correctly distinguishes GDP from GNI?
options: GDP = inside the borders; GNI = earned by citizens
GDP = earned by citizens; GNI = inside the borders
questions.expected: GDP = inside the borders; GNI = earned by citizens
questions.memo: GDP is location-based; GNI is nationality-based.

questions.question: Build a short answer on the difference between GDP and GNI.
questions.prompt: How do GDP and GNI differ?

options.text: GDP counts output inside the borders; GNI counts income of citizens
GDP and GNI measure exactly the same thing
A foreign firm's SA output is in GDP; a citizen's foreign income is in GNI
A citizen's foreign income is in GDP
So they differ by the net income flowing to and from abroad
So they can never differ at all

questions.memo: GDP = location-based; GNI = nationality-based.

ECON.G10.T1.BUSCYCLE.A1.title: Business cycles
ECON.G10.T1.BUSCYCLE.A1.description: The phases and indicators of business cycles, South African cycles, measuring them, exogenous and endogenous causes, and their effects on growth, employment and the vulnerable.
ECON.G10.T1.BUSCYCLE.A1.strand: Term 1 — Macroeconomics: basic concepts, the economic problem & the circular flow
ECON.G10.T1.BUSCYCLE.A1.recovery_strategy: One cycle runs trough → recovery → peak (boom) → recession → next trough.

questions.question: The regular ups and downs in economic activity over time are called the ______ cycle.
questions.memo: The business cycle is the wave of expansions and contractions.

questions.question: The lowest point of a business cycle is the…
questions.memo: The trough is the bottom, before recovery begins.

questions.question: The highest point of a business cycle is the…
questions.memo: The peak/boom is the top of the cycle before a downturn.

questions.question: During a boom, employment usually rises.
questions.memo: Booms bring more production and more jobs.

questions.question: A period of falling economic activity is called a ______.
questions.memo: A recession is a downswing in activity.

questions.question: On the business-cycle diagram, which label marks the BOOM?
options: The highest point of the wave
The lowest point of the wave
questions.expected: The highest point of the wave

source.caption: Business-cycle wave on a trend line.

questions.memo: The boom/peak is the top of the wave.

questions.question: On the diagram, the straight line through the middle of the wave is the…

source.caption: Business-cycle wave on a trend line.

questions.memo: The trend line shows the economy's long-run growth path.

questions.question: An 'exogenous' cause of business cycles comes from…
options: outside the economy, like a war or oil-price shock
inside the economy, like business confidence
questions.expected: outside the economy, like a war or oil-price shock
questions.memo: Exogenous = from outside; endogenous = from inside the system.

questions.question: An 'endogenous' cause of business cycles comes from…
options: inside the economy, like changes in investment or confidence
outside the economy, like the weather
questions.expected: inside the economy, like changes in investment or confidence
questions.memo: Endogenous causes arise within the economy itself.

questions.question: Sort each phase by whether activity is rising or falling.
questions.memo: Recovery and boom = rising; recession and slump = falling.

questions.question: Put one full business cycle in order, starting from the bottom.
questions.memo: From the bottom: recover up to a peak, then recede back down.

questions.question: During a recession, unemployment usually rises.
questions.memo: Less production in a recession means fewer jobs.

questions.question: Which is a typical effect of a boom?
questions.memo: Strong demand in a boom can push prices up.

questions.question: Business cycles hurt the economically vulnerable most during a…
questions.memo: Downturns hit low-income and casual workers hardest through job losses.

questions.question: Why do economists watch business cycles closely?
options: To help government time its policies and plan ahead
To set the price of bread
questions.expected: To help government time its policies and plan ahead
questions.memo: Knowing the cycle helps policymakers respond at the right time.

questions.question: A sharp, deep and long recession is best called a…
questions.memo: A severe, prolonged downturn is a depression.

questions.question: If business confidence collapses and firms stop investing, the cycle will most likely…
questions.memo: Falling investment (an endogenous cause) pushes activity down.

questions.question: The trend line shows short-term jumps, while the cycle shows the long-run path.
questions.memo: It is the reverse: the trend is the long-run path; the cycle is the short-run wave around it.

questions.question: Sort each cause as exogenous or endogenous.
questions.memo: Outside the economy = exogenous; inside = endogenous.

questions.question: Build a short answer on the effects of a recession.
questions.prompt: What happens to the economy during a recession?

options.text: A recession is a period of falling economic activity
A recession is a period of rising economic activity
Output falls and unemployment rises
Output rises and unemployment falls
The economically vulnerable suffer most as jobs and incomes are lost
Everyone becomes richer during a recession

questions.memo: Recession = falling output, rising unemployment, hardship for the vulnerable.

ECON.G10.T2.DEMSUP.A1.title: Demand, supply & price formation
ECON.G10.T2.DEMSUP.A1.description: Demand and supply, how equilibrium price and quantity are set, and the meaning of value, price and utility.
ECON.G10.T2.DEMSUP.A1.strand: Term 2 — Microeconomics: markets, the PPC & the public sector
ECON.G10.T2.DEMSUP.A1.recovery_strategy: Price change → MOVEMENT along the curve; a non-price factor → SHIFT of the whole curve.

questions.question: The law of demand says that, all else equal, when price rises, quantity demanded…
questions.memo: Higher prices discourage buying — demand slopes downward.

questions.question: The law of supply says that, all else equal, when price rises, quantity supplied…
questions.memo: Higher prices encourage producers to supply more.

questions.question: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is the ______ price.
questions.memo: Equilibrium is where the demand and supply curves cross.

questions.question: At a price above equilibrium there is usually a surplus.
questions.memo: Too-high prices mean supply exceeds demand — a surplus.

questions.question: At a price below equilibrium there is usually a shortage.
questions.memo: Too-low prices mean demand exceeds supply — a shortage.

questions.question: On the demand-and-supply graph, the equilibrium is found where…
options: the demand and supply curves cross
the demand curve meets the price axis
questions.expected: the demand and supply curves cross

source.caption: Demand and supply curves crossing at equilibrium.

questions.memo: Equilibrium price and quantity are at the intersection.

questions.question: On the graph, the downward-sloping line is the…

source.caption: Demand and supply curves crossing at equilibrium.

questions.memo: Demand slopes down; supply slopes up.

questions.question: A change in the good's own PRICE causes…
options: a shift of the whole curve
questions.memo: Own-price changes move you along the curve; other factors shift it.

questions.question: Which would SHIFT the demand curve for coffee to the right?
options: A rise in the coffee price
A fall in the coffee price
questions.memo: Higher income (a non-price factor) raises demand at every price.

questions.question: On the diagram, when demand shifts to the RIGHT, the equilibrium price…

source.caption: A rightward shift of the demand curve.

questions.memo: Higher demand pushes both price and quantity up.

questions.question: Sort each: does it cause a MOVEMENT along demand, or a SHIFT of demand?
questions.memo: Own price → movement; everything else → shift.

questions.question: Value, price and utility: 'utility' means…
questions.memo: Utility is the usefulness or satisfaction from consuming a good.

questions.question: If both demand and supply rise, the quantity traded will rise.
questions.memo: Both curves shifting right increases the equilibrium quantity.

questions.question: A shortage tends to push the price…
questions.memo: When buyers compete for too few goods, price rises toward equilibrium.

questions.question: Why does a free market tend to move toward equilibrium?
options: Surpluses push price down and shortages push price up until they clear
questions.expected: Surpluses push price down and shortages push price up until they clear
questions.memo: Price adjusts until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.question: A new health report makes people want less sugar. For sugar this is a…
questions.memo: Worse tastes for sugar lower demand at every price — a left shift.

questions.question: Bad weather destroys part of the maize crop. In the maize market this…
questions.memo: Less supply at every price raises the equilibrium price.

questions.question: A change in the price of a good shifts that good's own demand curve.
questions.memo: A change in the good's own price is a movement ALONG the curve, not a shift.

questions.question: Two learners explain a price rise.

source_a.text: Learner A: 'The price of tomatoes rose because a frost cut the supply.'

source_b.text: Learner B: 'The price of tomatoes rose because a TV chef made them popular, raising demand.'

statements.text: Describes a leftward shift of supply
Describes a rightward shift of demand

questions.memo: Both can raise price — one cuts supply, the other lifts demand.

questions.question: Build a short answer on how price is set in a market.
questions.prompt: How is the market price of a good determined?

options.text: Price is set where demand equals supply (equilibrium)
Price is set only by the seller's wishes
Above equilibrium there is a surplus; below it there is a shortage
Surpluses and shortages never affect price
Price adjusts until the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer
Price stays fixed no matter what buyers and sellers do

questions.memo: Equilibrium price clears the market — demand meets supply.

ECON.G10.T2.MKTTYPES.A1.title: Types & functions of markets
ECON.G10.T2.MKTTYPES.A1.description: Product vs factor markets, perfect vs imperfect markets, world markets, and the functions of markets (bringing demand and supply together, allocating resources, self-regulation).
ECON.G10.T2.MKTTYPES.A1.strand: Term 2 — Microeconomics: markets, the PPC & the public sector
ECON.G10.T2.MKTTYPES.A1.recovery_strategy: Perfect markets: many buyers/sellers, identical product, free entry. One seller = monopoly (imperfect).

questions.question: A market is best described as…
options: any place or system where buyers and sellers trade
questions.expected: any place or system where buyers and sellers trade
questions.memo: A market is wherever buyers and sellers interact, including online.

questions.question: The product market is where people buy and sell…
questions.memo: Product markets trade finished goods and services.

questions.question: The factor market is where people buy and sell…
options: factors of production like labour and land
questions.expected: factors of production like labour and land
questions.memo: Factor markets trade the inputs used to produce goods.

questions.question: In a perfect market there are many buyers and sellers and an identical product.
questions.memo: Perfect competition has many traders and a homogeneous product.

questions.question: A market with only ONE seller is a ______.
questions.memo: One seller = a monopoly, an imperfect market.

questions.question: Which is a function of markets?
questions.memo: Markets coordinate buyers and sellers and allocate resources.

questions.question: Markets help 'allocate resources' by…
options: sending resources to where they are most valued via prices
questions.expected: sending resources to where they are most valued via prices
questions.memo: Prices guide resources to their most valued uses.

ECON.G10.T2.PPC.A1.title: Production possibility curve

questions.question: On a PPC of 'guns vs butter', producing more guns means…

questions.expected: shift the PPC outward over time

giving up one good for the other

ECON.G10.T2.PUBSEC.A1.title: Public sector intervention

questions.question: A government payment to producers to lower costs and prices is a ______.
questions.memo: A subsidy supports producers and can lower prices.

questions.memo: At the high floor price, supply outstrips demand by the surplus.

ECON.G10.T3.GLOBHIST.A1.title: Growth, development & globalisation in history

questions.memo: Retail and banking are tertiary (services).

ECON.G11.T2.ELAST.A1.title: Price elasticity

questions.question: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in ______.

questions.question: Demand is 'inelastic' when…
options: quantity barely responds to a price change (elasticity < 1)
questions.expected: quantity barely responds to a price change (elasticity < 1)
questions.memo: Inelastic demand reacts weakly to price.

questions.memo: People keep buying necessities even when prices rise.

questions.question: On the diagram, the steeper demand curve is…

questions.memo: Income elasticity links quantity demanded to income changes.

questions.question: Cross elasticity of demand measures the response of one good's quantity to a change in…
questions.memo: Cross elasticity links one good's demand to another's price.

questions.memo: When one substitute's price rises, demand for the other rises — positive cross elasticity.

questions.question: If a good has elastic demand, a price CUT will tend to…

questions.question: If a good has inelastic demand, a price RISE will tend to…

questions.expected: Buyers easily switch away when its price rises

questions.memo: Diminishing marginal utility: extra units give less added satisfaction.

Elastic and inelastic demand react exactly the same

ECON.G11.T2.MKTREL.A1.title: Relationships between markets

questions.memo: Cheaper petrol makes driving large cars more attractive.

questions.question: Relative prices guide consumers by showing…

questions.memo: Relative prices help buyers compare and choose.
